source: Smith, Ward and Schumacher (1993) Constraining effects of examples in a creative generation task
finding: Seeing three example creatures or toys made later designs share the examples' features. Idea count did not change, so the cost was in content, not quantity.
numbers: Exp 1 N=94: overall conformity higher with examples for toys F(1,92)=8.13 and creatures F(1,92)=12.50. About 3 toys and 3.5 creatures per person in both groups (F<1).
quote: Recent experience can lead to unintentional conformity, constraining the generation of creative ideas.
limits: Students, 20-minute sketch tasks, features chosen by the authors (ball, tail, four legs). Conformity to named features, not a rating of originality.
agent_relevance: Any example shown in the prompt will leak its features into the output. Examples are a cost in the generate phase, so S3 should start without prior answers in view, or with examples of what to avoid.

source: Smith, Ward and Schumacher (1993) Constraining effects of examples in a creative generation task
finding: A 23-minute filler task between the examples and the generation task did not remove conformity. The apparent drop with delay was an order effect.
numbers: Exp 2 N=91, 2x2 (examples vs control x immediate vs delayed). Order/delay effect on overall creature conformity F(1,87)=4.61; the authors call it an order effect, not a decline in example-induced conformity.
limits: Same lab and materials as Exp 1. The delay was filled with another generation task.
agent_relevance: A break or an unrelated task between exposure and generation does not cleanse the influence. Use a fresh context with no examples instead.

source: Smith, Ward and Schumacher (1993) Constraining effects of examples in a creative generation task
finding: This experiment tells two rival explanations apart. The memory view says conformity is unintentional and cannot be told away. The subject-bias view says people copy because they think they should. Telling people to be different did not remove the copying, and telling them to copy raised it.
numbers: Exp 3 N=80, four groups. Tail proportion: control .16, standard examples .34, diverge .53, conform .62 (read from Table 4). Overall conformity F(3,76)=8.69. Control vs diverge t(76)=2.89 (still more conformity). Control vs standard only marginal, t(76)=1.56.
quote: Explicitly instructing subjects to create ideas that were very different from the examples did not decrease conformity.
limits: Control vs standard was only marginal in this experiment, so the effect size is modest. Creature task only.
agent_relevance: Instruction like 'be different from the examples' is weak. Diversity has to come from code (what the model is shown, rejection of near copies), not from asking. Fits G4 and G8.

source: Marsh, Landau and Hicks (1996) How examples may (and may not) constrain creativity
finding: The conformity effect replicated in all three experiments, but it did not shrink total output, elaborateness, or the number of non-critical novel features. So conformity is real, but it did not prove a loss of creative output.
numbers: Exp 1 N=80 (16 per group, 0, 1, 3, 6 or 9 examples). Critical features were 4.4% of features in controls and 12.1% with nine examples (6.6 vs 7.1 features per creature). Number of creatures and novel features did not vary (F(4,75)<1).
quote: Conformity was observed in all three experiments; ... did not confirm that the conformity effect constrained creative output.
limits: Abstract, introduction and Experiment 1 results read. Experiments 2 and 3 only through the abstract and a few lines. Creature drawing task, students.
agent_relevance: Copying a feature is not the same as losing novelty. Measure novelty on the whole output, not only overlap with a shown example.

source: Marsh, Landau and Hicks (1996) How examples may (and may not) constrain creativity
finding: More examples gave more conformity in a dose-response way. Common Earth-animal features dropped as examples increased, while novel features stayed constant at about 6 to 7 features per creature.
numbers: Exp 1: linear trend significant for tail (omnibus F(4,75)=3.65, p<.01) and four legs (F(4,75)=2.73, p<.05); antennae not significant (F(4,75)=1.46, p=.224). Groups saw 0, 1, 3, 6, 9 examples.
limits: Small groups of 16. Only three critical features were scored.
agent_relevance: Each extra shown example adds pull. Keep the shown set small, or show examples that differ from each other on the dimension that matters.

source: Marsh, Landau and Hicks (1996) How examples may (and may not) constrain creativity
finding: Examples whose features covaried in ways that never occur together in nature led to higher subjective creativity ratings (Exp 2). A delay between examples and test increased conformity (Exp 3), as models of inadvertent plagiarism predict. This conflicts with the null delay effect in Smith et al. Exp 2.
numbers: Exp 2 and 3 from the abstract only. No cell means recorded.
quote: A delay between presentation and test increased conformity (Experiment 3).
limits: Abstract only for Exp 2 and 3. The delay moderator is unsettled between the two papers.
agent_relevance: Unsettled: whether delay washes out or worsens copying. Test it with the model (same prompt with examples early vs late in a long context).

source: Marsh, Landau and Hicks (1996) How examples may (and may not) constrain creativity
finding: Four rival accounts of the conformity effect are compared: activation, retrieval blocking, structured imagination (path of least resistance), and category abstraction. No experiment cleanly separates all four.
numbers: Introduction text only. Reports Ward 1994: people designing non-Earth creatures still produced bilateral symmetry, sense organs and limbs; with a lava planet they added wings, not jet engines; the 'beyond your wildest imagination' instruction did not remove this.
quote: Instructions ... did not diminish this regularity and the structured nature of their creative output.
limits: Secondary report of Ward (1994); the original was not read.
agent_relevance: A strong prior (Earth animals) shapes output whatever the instruction says. For an LLM the prior is the training distribution, so engineer variation outside the prompt text.

source: Christensen and Schunn (2007) The relationship of analogical distance to analogical function and preinventive structure: the case of engineering design
finding: In a real engineering design team, designers made fewer distant (between-domain) analogies when they talked about a physical prototype than about a bare idea or a sketch.
numbers: Segments: idea N=1,616, sketch 220, prototype 1,383. Ideas had more analogies than prototypes, chi2(1)=7.88, p=.006. Analogical distance by structure type chi2(2)=19.26, p=.001. Between-domain share lower for prototypes than ideas (Fisher p<.001) and than sketches (p=.019); sketches did not differ from ideas (p=1.0).
quote: reference to exemplars (in the form of prototypes) significantly reduced the number of between-domain analogies
limits: One team, in vivo, coded transcripts (kappa .71 to 1.0). Not randomised.
agent_relevance: Once a concrete runnable artifact exists, far analogies thin out. Keep the wide idea stage (S3) apart from the run stage (S4) so early running does not narrow the search.

source: Christensen and Schunn (2007) The relationship of analogical distance to analogical function and preinventive structure: the case of engineering design
finding: Analogies in design were about 55% within-domain and 45% between-domain, and served three jobs: identifying problems, solving them, and explaining them.
numbers: 28% of analogy segments identified problems, 40% solved problems, 32% explained. Problem-identifying analogies mainly within-domain, explanatory ones mainly between-domain.
limits: Single design team.
agent_relevance: Far analogies are used mostly to explain, not to solve. Do not expect distant sources to give working solutions; check them by running (G8).

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Head to head: LLM-generated ideas were rated more novel than ideas by expert researchers, on topic-matched, style-normalised ideas. The pipeline was generate many, remove duplicates, rank.
numbers: 49 idea writers, 79 reviewers, 298 unique reviews. Novelty mean: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI plus human rerank 5.81 (Welch t-test, Bonferroni, p<0.01, per-review Test 1). Reviews per condition: human 119, AI 109, rerank 109. Overall score human 4.68, AI 4.85, rerank 5.34 (p=0.04, rerank only). Result held across three statistical tests.
quote: LLM-generated ideas are judged as more novel (p < 0.05) than human expert ideas while being judged slightly weaker on feasibility.
limits: One field (prompting research in NLP), judged by reviewers, not by execution. Reviewer agreement only 56.1%.
agent_relevance: Generate widely then filter beats a single human draft on judged novelty. But judged novelty is not a test by running (G8).

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: The generate phase saturates. Out of 4,000 seed ideas per topic only about 5% (about 200) were non-duplicates at cosine threshold 0.8.
numbers: 4,000 seed ideas per topic, dedup at similarity 0.8; accumulated non-duplicates plateau as more batches are generated.
limits: Duplicate threshold is a design choice and embeddings come from one model.
agent_relevance: More sampling from one prompt gives repeats, not new structures. Budget the width of S3 and add diversity by changing the input, not by sampling more.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: A model used as the final selector of ideas did no better than chance. Human reviewers agreed with each other only modestly, and LLM judges agreed with them less.
numbers: Balanced accuracy on top vs bottom 25% of ideas: expert inter-reviewer 56.1%; best LLM judge (own pairwise ranker, Claude-3.5) 53.3%; GPT-4o direct 50.0, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0 (read from figure). NeurIPS 2021 reviewers 66.0%, ICLR 2024 LM papers 71.9%.
limits: The task is judging unexecuted ideas, where even experts disagree.
agent_relevance: Supports G5 and G8: the generating model is not a usable final selector. Selection needs a check that runs.

source: Si, Hashimoto and Yang (2025) The ideation-execution gap: execution outcomes of LLM-generated versus human research ideas
finding: When 43 experts actually executed the ideas, the novelty edge of LLM ideas disappeared and on many metrics reversed. The explore-by-running step undid the advantage seen at generation.
numbers: 43 experts, over 100 hours each, 4-page papers reviewed blind. Scores of LLM ideas fell significantly more than human ideas on novelty, excitement, effectiveness and overall (p<0.05). Rankings flipped for many metrics.
quote: However, a good idea should not simply appear to be novel, it should also result in better research after being executed.
limits: Abstract page read; full text not opened. Small N, one field, expert-executed.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for the Geneplore split: the explore phase changes the verdict on a preinventive idea. Judge by execution, not by how the idea sounds (G8).

source: Gupta and Pruthi (2025) All that glitters is not novel: plagiarism in AI generated research
finding: Experts told to look for copying found that a quarter of LLM-generated research proposals were paraphrases of, or heavily borrowed from, existing papers. Automated detectors missed them.
numbers: 13 experts, 50 documents (36 newly generated with the Si pipeline at 500 ideas per topic, plus 14 exemplars). 14.0% scored 5 (direct copy) and 10.0% scored 4: 24% plagiarised; 36% if unverified claims are counted. Source-paper authors cross-verified.
limits: Small N. Experts were told to presume plagiarism (a deliberate bias). Includes exemplar documents chosen by earlier authors.
agent_relevance: A model that sounds novel may only be recombining known work. Novelty needs a code search of known work (G8), not the model's word.

source: Gupta and Pruthi (2025) All that glitters is not novel: plagiarism in AI generated research
finding: This is a rival reading of the Si 2024 result: the same kind of pipeline, but searching for sources changes the verdict from novel to borrowed in a quarter of cases.
numbers: Same pipeline code as Si et al. with 500 not 4,000 ideas per topic. Plagiarism detectors tested on synthetic plagiarism were also inadequate.
limits: Our inference from comparing two papers; not a direct replication.
agent_relevance: Part of the judged novelty in LLM idea pipelines may be unrecognised borrowing.

source: Wang, Downey, Ji and Hope (2024) SciMON: scientific inspiration machines optimized for novelty
finding: A loop that retrieves related prior work, compares the idea to it, and rewrites until it is less similar raised novelty in many cases, but mostly by combining popular concepts.
numbers: Round 1: 88.9% of updated ideas substantially different, 55.6% judged more novel. Round 2: more novel for 57.8% of ideas carried on. Novelty did not drop where it failed to rise. Ground-truth paper ideas judged higher in technical level in 85% of comparisons with GPT4 variants. GPT4 plus knowledge graph less incremental in 45% of pairs.
limits: Five to six volunteer raters. Ideas grew longer after boosting and GPT-4 output length may bias preference. Domain: NLP and biomedical idea sentences.
agent_relevance: A retrieve-compare-rewrite loop is a code-driven generate then explore. It lifts novelty but not depth; pair with a run check.

source: Meincke, Mollick and Terwiesch (2024) Prompting diverse ideas: increasing AI idea variance
finding: GPT-4 idea pools are less diverse than pools from groups of people, and prompt choice shifts diversity only a little. Writing a long list and then revising for boldness came closest to humans.
numbers: Mean pairwise cosine similarity (lower is more diverse): human group 0.243; GPT-4 prompts 0.255 to 0.432; base prompt 0.377; 'think like Steve Jobs' 0.368; HBR creativity tools 0.387. 35 prompts, 10 runs of 100 ideas each. Differences significant by bootstrap and permutation (p<0.01), with authors' caution on cosine measures.
limits: One task (product ideas for students under $50). Cosine similarity of embeddings is not a human diversity rating. About 15% of CoT runs removed because the model skipped the revise step.
agent_relevance: Generate then revise in one prompt chain lifts diversity. Compare it with code-forced diversity.

source: Meincke, Mollick and Terwiesch (2024) Prompting diverse ideas: increasing AI idea variance
finding: The Chain-of-Thought generate-then-revise prompt enlarged the reachable idea space and slowed repeats. Its edge was strongest in the first few hundred ideas and gone by about 750.
numbers: Estimated idea space: base prompt about 3,700 unique ideas with 13.8% repeats; CoT about 4,700 with 11.7% repeats. CoT advantage in cosine similarity strongest between 100 and 500 ideas, negligible after about 750 to 800.
limits: Single task and model (GPT-4, 2023). The opportunity-space estimate depends on the 0.8 cosine threshold.
agent_relevance: Pays off at modest width. Past a few hundred samples, extra width from the same prompt adds little.

source: Hubert, Awa and Zabelina (2024) The current state of artificial intelligence generative language models is more creative than humans on divergent thinking tasks
finding: With fluency matched, GPT-4 scored higher than 151 people on word-distance originality and on elaboration across three divergent-thinking tasks.
numbers: 151 humans (Prolific) vs GPT-4 sessions. AUT originality group effect F(1,600)=622.10, p<0.001, effect size 0.51; fluency matched (human 6.94, GPT-4 7.01). Divergent Association Task semantic distance: GPT-4 84.56 (SD 3.05) vs humans 76.95 (SD 6.13). Elaboration in the Consequences task: GPT-4 38.69 words vs 5.45.
limits: Originality scored by GloVe semantic distance, which rewards unusual words and long answers. No usefulness rating or feasibility check.
agent_relevance: Semantic-distance originality is easy for a model to win and does not show real-world novelty. Do not use embedding distance alone as the novelty gate.

source: Ashkinaze, Mendelsohn, Qiwei, Budak and Gilbert (2025) How AI ideas affect the creativity, diversity, and evolution of human ideas: evidence from a large, dynamic experiment
finding: Showing people many ChatGPT ideas before they brainstormed made the group's ideas more varied, but did not make any single idea more creative. A few AI ideas did nothing.
numbers: 800+ participants, 40+ countries, over 3,000 responses. Global diversity higher in high-exposure conditions: disclosed beta=0.31 (p=0.001), undisclosed beta=0.26 (p=0.001) vs control. No effect of low exposure and no main effect of disclosure.
quote: AI made ideas different, not better.
limits: Alternate Uses style task, SBERT embeddings for diversity. Recruited mostly from a creativity-interest newsletter.
agent_relevance: Exposure to outside ideas can widen the set (a source of variation) without improving each idea. Good for S3 breadth; the S4 test is still needed to find the good ones.

source: Wang, Okada and Takagi (2023) How to effectively overcome fixation: a systematic review of fixation and defixation studies
finding: A review of 53 experiments says defixation raises solution rates on closed problems, but on open-ended (creative) problems it does not automatically improve results; work inside the existing frame can also help.
numbers: 53 experimental studies sorted by fixation source and problem type (closed vs open ended).
limits: Systematic review without a pooled effect size. Studies measure different outcomes.
agent_relevance: Do not assume that breaking fixation (forcing far ideas) equals better ideas. Measure both fixation and quality.

source: Wang, Okada and Takagi (2023) How to effectively overcome fixation: a systematic review of fixation and defixation studies
finding: Warning people not to copy flawed example features is unreliable. Jansson and Smith (1991) and Viswanathan and Linsey found no effect; Chrysikou and Weisberg (2005) replicated with an effect.
numbers: Instruction failed in Jansson & Smith (1991), Viswanathan & Linsey (2013a,b) and Viswanathan et al. (2014); it relaxed fixation in Chrysikou & Weisberg (2005). Candidate moderators: group vs individual testing; psychology students vs engineering students and professionals.
limits: Described through this review, not read in the originals. Participant expertise is a plausible moderator, not shown.
agent_relevance: Instructions to avoid are weak and depend on who the solver is. For the model, test per task rather than assume.

source: Wang, Okada and Takagi (2023) How to effectively overcome fixation: a systematic review of fixation and defixation studies
finding: Warnings that mention examples can activate them. Warnings that describe the example at a higher level of abstraction reduced fixation and raised originality (Ezzat et al., 2020).
numbers: Ezzat et al. 2020 as reported; partial-photo examples raised originality (Cheng et al. 2014), but the review notes originality alone cannot tell if fixation changed.
quote: mentioning examples in warning instructions may paradoxically act as a trigger that activates related knowledge
limits: Secondary report only; no numbers in the review text for these studies.
agent_relevance: Abstract the example before showing it, rather than stating it plainly and saying not to copy it.

source: Mukherjee and Chang (2023) The creative frontier of generative AI: managing the novelty-usefulness tradeoff
finding: A conceptual paper argues that pushing novelty alone yields hallucination and pushing usefulness alone yields memorisation. It offers a framework and no experiment.
numbers: No data. Five-part framework: domain analysis, transfer learning, user preferences, custom metrics, collaboration.
limits: Position paper with no tests. It only states the novelty vs usefulness tension.
agent_relevance: Names the trade-off our gate must manage; gives no evidence about how.

source: Gu, Zhang, Wang and Li (2024) LLMs can realize combinatorial creativity: generating creative ideas via LLMs for scientific research
finding: A framework that retrieves concepts at different abstraction levels and recombines them was reported to beat baselines at generating research ideas on OAG-Bench.
numbers: Abstract only: reports consistent gains over baselines; no numbers recorded.
limits: Abstract read only. Metrics unknown to us, probably model-judged or reference-based.
agent_relevance: Abstraction-level retrieval is a candidate way to pick sources for recombination. Test before adopting.

source: Finke and Slayton (1988) Explorations of creative visual synthesis in mental imagery
finding: People given three random parts (shapes, lines, characters) and asked to imagine combining them found a recognisable pattern on about 40% of trials. Few results could be predicted from the parts alone.
numbers: About 40% success per trial across two experiments. Parts given with no assembly instructions. Most subjects said a pattern emerged after trying combinations.
quote: These findings show that visual discoveries in imagery can be reliably induced under appropriate laboratory conditions.
limits: Abstract and first page only (the PDF copy was removed from the shared scratch folder before I read the rest). Visual imagery, not verbal or code. No comparison group without the parts.
agent_relevance: The root effect for the model's open mode: random combinations plus an interpret step find things the parts do not predict. A reason to test random-seed recombination checked by running.

source: Heinonen, Numminen, Hlushchuk, Antell, Taatila and Suomala (2016) Default mode and executive networks areas: association with the serial order in divergent thinking
finding: In a mental Alternative Uses task, participants produced 22 to 148 ideas for 11 household objects. Serial order was measured by response time; originality was not recorded because the scanner blocked answers.
numbers: Mean 71.06 ideas (SD 32.88) in the scanner. fMRI model with a serial-order predictor.
limits: The authors say they could not evaluate originality in the scanner. The brain-network result is about people. Only introduction, methods and limits read.
agent_relevance: Only a pointer: the claim that later ideas are more original is not tested on originality here.

source: Replication of Finke (1990) with a preinventive play condition (course project page, University of Colorado)
finding: A student replication of Finke's preinventive-form experiment, with a third preinventive play condition, found no differences between conditions. A second description says the preinventive phase raised originality at a cost to practicality in a physical-synthesis version.
numbers: Search-result snippet only. The wiki page returned a 503 error four times and the Wayback copy does not exist. No N or means seen.
limits: Not opened. Not peer reviewed. Cannot verify N, scoring or statistics. The 'originality up, practicality down' line contradicts the 'no differences' line within the same sources.
agent_relevance: Treat as an unverified failure to replicate. The claim in SUBFIELDS that the preinventive phase raised originality is not confirmed by anything we could open.

source: Kwon et al. (Berkeley CoDesign) Generating preinventive structures: AI-driven creativity in product repurposing
finding: A multimodal model made preinventive structures (combinations of parts of an existing product); some of them appeared in real repurposing designs (IKEA hacks).
numbers: Abstract page only: no N and no novelty or usefulness numbers on the page.
limits: Abstract only. Overlap with human hacks shows reachability, not novelty or usefulness.
agent_relevance: The nearest direct LLM analogue of a preinventive structure: a part combination proposed before the use is known. Full paper needed to learn whether it was run or only compared.
